moments.title: A castle for the waterworks
moments.text: Architect William W. Boyington's Gothic-style limestone tower was finished to hide a 138-foot standpipe for the pumping station across the street, part of a new system that drew water from the Two-Mile Crib.

moments.title: It survives the Great Fire
moments.text: The stone tower and the pumping station were among the few structures in the burned district to come through the fire.

moments.title: The standpipe goes out of use
moments.text: Changes to the water system made the tower's standpipe obsolete, but the city kept the building.

moments.title: Named a Chicago Landmark
moments.text: The city designated the Water Tower a Chicago Landmark.

moments.title: A city art gallery opens inside
moments.text: The city began using the tower as the City Gallery, with free art and photography exhibitions.

moments.title: Today: a landmark on the Magnificent Mile
moments.text: The tower still stands at Michigan and Chicago avenues, surrounded by shops and high-rises. The city lists its gallery as closed.

sources.title: Chicago Water Tower, Historic American Buildings Survey (Library of Congress)
City Gallery in the Historic Water Tower (City of Chicago)

checked.notes: Completed 1869 by W. W. Boyington; limestone; 138-foot standpipe for the pumping station; survived the 1871 fire; obsolete by 1906 (Britannica, Library of Congress HABS, Wikipedia). Chicago Landmark 1971 per one source. The 1999 start of the City Gallery comes from a blog and is weakly sourced. The city's gallery page now says the gallery is closed, so the 'today' line was changed from 'now a free city art gallery'.
